## What "15 February 1750/1" means

This is a **double-dated year** — a notation clerks used in England during the period when the civil year began on **25 March** (Lady Day), not 1 January.

Here's the logic:

| Layer | What it means |
|---|---|
| **1750** | The Old Style civil year — the year England's legal calendar was still "in" on 15 February |
| **1751** | The New Style year — the year by modern reckoning (1 January start) |

February falls *between* 1 January and 25 March, which is exactly the window where the two years diverge. The clerk wrote both to prevent ambiguity, which was good practice at the time.

---

## Which year to use in your notes

**Record 1751** — the New Style year — as the resolved date.

The tool confirms: **15 February 1750 O.S. → 15 February 1751 N.S.**

The day (15 February) stays the same; only the year changes.

---

## How to write it in your notes

Use this format to be transparent about the source and your interpretation:

> **15 February 1750/1 (O.S.)** — recorded as dual-dated; resolved to **15 February 1751 (N.S.)**

This matters because:
- **Placing it in 1750** would put it 6 weeks *before* the actual event by modern reckoning — a real error if you're building a timeline.
- England switched fully to the Gregorian calendar in **September 1752**, so any English record before that date in the Jan–Mar window may carry this notation.

## Why February 30 existed in Sweden

Sweden spent 1700–1712 on its own one-off calendar — neither Julian nor Gregorian — because of a failed gradual transition:

1. **1700** — Sweden skipped its leap day, planning to drop leap days every 4 years for 40 years to drift quietly onto the Gregorian calendar.
2. **1704 & 1708** — Sweden forgot, added the leap days back, and ended up stranded: *one day ahead of Julian, ten days behind Gregorian.*
3. **1712** — Sweden gave up and decided to snap back to the Julian calendar. To do so, it needed to *add* a day it had previously removed. So it made February 1712 have **both** February 29 **and** February 30. That extra day existed in Sweden and nowhere else on Earth.
4. **1753** — Sweden finally, cleanly, switched to the Gregorian calendar (skipping 11 days: 17 Feb was followed by 1 Mar 1753).

---

The date **30 February 1712, Stockholm** is genuine. It corresponds to **11 March 1712 (Gregorian)**. When citing or entering it in your tree, preserve the original date as recorded — it is historically significant — and note the Gregorian equivalent alongside it.

## "25 March 1750/1" — an anomalous slash date

### What double-dated years normally mean

In England before 1752, the legal year began on **25 March (Lady Day)**, not 1 January. Clerks writing dates between **1 January and 24 March** often showed *both* years with a slash — the legal (Old Style) year that hadn't turned over yet, and the historical (New Style) year that had already begun on 1 January by modern reckoning. So "6 January 1750/1" is straightforwardly read as 1751 in modern notes.

---

### Why this date is different — and needs checking

**25 March is Lady Day itself** — the very day the Old Style year incremented. The double-dating window is **1 January through 24 March only**. On 25 March, the Old Style and New Style years agree: the new year has begun by both reckonings simultaneously. A slash written on that exact date is **anomalous**, and the tool declined to resolve it for that reason.

> *"A slash written outside the window is anomalous — check where the year turns over in the surrounding register entries rather than resolving it."*

---

### What to do in your research notes

1. **Don't assume 1751.** The standard double-date rule doesn't apply here.
2. **Check the surrounding entries** in the same register. Find where the clerk's year turns over — does the entry immediately before read 1750, and entries shortly after read 1751? That context tells you what the clerk intended.
3. **Record what the source says.** In your notes, write the date exactly as found: *25 March 1750/1*, with a note that it's anomalous and you checked surrounding entries.
4. **Once you confirm intent from context**, record the year accordingly — most likely 1751, but the register itself must confirm it.

---

**Short answer:** This slash shouldn't be there on 25 March. Don't resolve it mechanically. Check the register's surrounding entries for where the year changes, then record the date as the clerk clearly intended.
